units.translation: But envious pain creeps upon the Atreidae, who are engaged in litigation.
Every manner of form leads the way.
to place under; (middle) to undertake, promise; to withstand
The middle form ὑφίσταμαι [I undertake] means "I take upon myself, I promise."
Thus Wellauer for ὑποστήσει [you will place under].
which the scholiast explains by ἀντιστὰς [having withstood], ἀντιμαχησάμενος [having fought against].
unless you will place some trust in this expedition.
and then you undertook to receive the new blood.
but no one who has withstood the great stream of men is approved.
of the tongue that is too boastful.
who struck him with his boastful vaunts.
The same author elsewhere said ὑψίκρημνος [steep, precipitous].

in Plutarch's Moralia p. 454 e, where Heathius reads ήβήσασα [having mounted], Paleius ἀμφιβᾶσα [having gone around], R. Ellis in The Journal of Philology, Cambridge 1868 p. 75 reads ὑβώσασα [having raised].
the long-robed train of the high roof.
having mounted the high work of the builders.
and the tall-grown branch of the olive.
It is also read in Homer's Epigrams 6, 5 and Nonnus' Dionysiaca 2, 454.
a city on a high cliff.
I came to Himera on a high cliff.
with high towers; towering like a tower
Figuratively, built up high like a tower
they then fortified this new city with high towers.
and he hurls mortals utterly destroyed from high-towered hopes (thus Hermann for δὲ ἀπιδὼν [but having looked away]).
highest; utmost, extreme; (of Zeus) most high
Of Jupiter, the highest of the gods. Sophocles Ph. 1289 said ἁγνὸν Ζηνὸς ὑψίστου σέβας [the holy majesty of highest Zeus]: for thus Wakefield corrected it for ἁγνοῦ ὕψιστον [holy highest].
before you come to the Caucasus itself, the highest of mountains.
I hear these are the very highest of evils.
where the highest of evils await them to suffer.
For fear is highest among mortals.
the holy majesty of highest Zeus
and from above may he hear well when called.
look at the watcher from above.
for a heron flying from above will strike you with its dung.
a height too great for leaping.
on high the end of the immortals will leave him.

Etymologicum Gudianum p. 316, 30, corrected from Paris codex 2638: κερδώ [the fox]: in diminutive form, as in Aeschylus (fr. 210) Εἰδώ [Eido] and Ὑψώ [Hypso] instead of Εἰδοθέα [Eidothea] and Ὑψιπύλη [Hypsipyle]. Cf. Bekker's Anecdota p. 857, 9 and the scholiast on Aristophanes' Knights 1065 (1068).
the fox: in diminutive form, as in Aeschylus
Eido and Hypso instead of Eidothea and Hypsipyle
